rows.label: raws-labs/tinycast, 512 history
rows.note: cut to 512 steps like ours (our run)

findings.title: Better than Toto-2.0-4m on our test sets, with 5× fewer parameters
findings.text: Our 0.87M student against the smallest official Toto: 6–8% lower error on fresh electricity, the shapes and held-out public data.
findings.takeaway: A small model trained on a big model's forecasts can beat a model of similar size trained from scratch by its authors.

findings.title: Level with the teacher it copies on our test sets
findings.text: Within 3% of Timestral-5M on electricity and public data, 2% better on the shapes, where half our training data comes from the same generators. On GIFT-Eval the teacher stays 18% ahead.
findings.takeaway: A student can match its teacher on data like its training windows; check far from them before claiming more.

findings.title: On GIFT-Eval it is still 3% behind Toto-2.0-4m
findings.versus: vs Toto-2.0-4m at the same 512-step context
findings.text: On 55 short-term GIFT-Eval configs our student is 3% worse than Toto-2.0-4m reading the same 512 steps, and wins 24 of them. Earlier 1M-window students were 9–11% behind: most of the gap closed with more training windows and a smaller teacher.
findings.takeaway: Distillation transfers the teacher's skill only on inputs like those you distil on. Test on data outside your training domain before claiming generality.

findings.title: A student trained on the domain's own history ties it on that domain
findings.versus: distilled general student vs a same-size student trained on 12k French electricity windows
findings.text: On electricity, a student trained only on real electricity history (plus synthetic series) scores the same. On the shapes the distilled student has 15% lower error: it is the general one.
findings.takeaway: If you only forecast one domain and have its history, train on it first. Distil when you need one model for many domains.

findings.title: Teacher forecasts are better labels than the real future
findings.versus: teacher labels vs real futures, same network, same 300k windows
findings.text: Only the training target changes: the teacher's 13 quantiles (Timestral-209M) instead of the one future that happened. The teacher's distribution is a less noisy target than a single draw.
findings.takeaway: With real inputs, train on the teacher's quantiles (α = 1), not on the observed values.

findings.title: More training windows is the biggest lever
findings.versus: 300k windows vs 30k, same student and teacher
findings.text: No other change we tested (teacher, loss, student size) moved the score as much.
findings.takeaway: Spend your compute on labelling more windows before tuning anything else.

findings.title: …and it keeps paying off at 1M windows
findings.text: Same student, labels from Timestral-28M. Gains on all three test sets, largest on the fresh electricity data.
findings.takeaway: If 300k windows helped, try 1M before changing the architecture.

findings.title: At 1M windows, the choice of teacher barely matters
findings.versus: Toto-2.0-313m labels vs Timestral-28M labels, same 1M windows
findings.text: Between −3% and +3% depending on the test set. An ensemble of three teachers was no better either, although it won by 2% at 30k windows.
findings.takeaway: Pick the teacher with the cleanest licence and the cheapest inference; scale the data instead.

findings.title: Random noise as input teaches nothing
findings.versus: white-noise inputs vs KernelSynth inputs, both labelled by the teacher
findings.text: On noise, the teacher answers every input with the same flat forecast, so the student learns one flat forecast. Gaussian-process series (KernelSynth) make the teacher react to trend and seasonality.
findings.takeaway: Data-free distillation works only with structured synthetic inputs.

findings.title: On synthetic inputs, the real future beats the teacher
findings.versus: teacher labels vs the generator's true future, synthetic inputs only
findings.text: When the generator knows the exact continuation, that continuation is a better target on the shapes than the teacher's guess; elsewhere it is a tie.
findings.takeaway: Distil where the truth is noisy (real data); use the generator's truth where it is exact.

findings.title: int8 is free on electricity, costs 3% on shapes
findings.versus: int8 ONNX vs fp32 ONNX, same student
findings.text: Dynamic int8 with per-channel weights, patch embedding kept in fp32: 3.6 MB → 1.2 MB.
findings.takeaway: Quantise, then re-run the benchmark: the parity error does not tell you the accuracy cost.

findings.title: Little history? Fine-tune from the distilled weights
findings.versus: fine-tune on 1 week of history: from distilled weights vs random weights (3 seeds)
findings.text: Measured with an earlier student (300k windows, Timestral-209M labels). On electricity, one week of data from random weights gives a model worse than seasonal naive.
findings.takeaway: Start every small-data fine-tune from the distilled checkpoint.

findings.title: With a full year of history, the head start is gone
findings.versus: fine-tune on 1 year: distilled weights vs random weights (3 seeds)
findings.text: Same earlier student. With enough in-domain data, training from scratch is as good or slightly better.
findings.takeaway: Distillation is worth most when your own data is scarce.
